header.title: Quaestiones medicae et problemata physica: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Cassius Iatrosophista
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tlg0733.tlg001.1st1K-grc1, from Open Greek and Latin's First1KGreek (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.

notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0733.tlg001.1st1K-gr: 1.1: περικειμένως is obscure; taken as 'with circumspection' (perhaps for περιεσκεμμένως). The clause καὶ ἐκ τούτων ἂν συμβαίη ἕλκῃ seems corrupt; rendered by sense. γωνιῶτχῆμα read as γωνιῶδες σχῆμα, ἐπιδιαιρέσες as ἐπιδιαιρέσεως. 6.1: 'the lying becomes greater' (μείζων ἡ κατάκλισις) makes poor sense; the text probably meant that the pain becomes greater. 8.1: ήδυμ read as ἥδυμον (Homer's epithet of sleep); μεθ’ γ̔δονῆς as μεθ’ ἡδονῆς; αἰσθτιὸν as αἰσθητικόν.

9.1: ἀπούλωσιν read as ἐπούλωσιν. 10.1: 'σύνοδον' (coming together) is obscure; possibly closure of the wound or of tissue. 11.1: συνεδεύοντος read as συνεδρεύοντος. 13.1: ἀνἀέχεται read as ἀνέχεται; the sentence 'or from joint growth' (ἢ ἐξ συναυξήσεως) seems intrusive and may be corrupt. 15.1: ἴποι read as εἴποι; 'ἐναποσκηπτικός' rendered 'causing deposits'. 17.1: the bracketed clause is an editorial supplement. 22.1: 'νοῦς ὁρᾷ' alludes to Epicharmus' 'mind sees, mind hears'; πρηγησαμένης read as προηγησαμένης; ἀντιαμβάνονται as ἀντιλαμβάνονται; φωνήσεως as φωνῆς. 23.1: the reasoning is compressed and the sense of μυσάντων (closed) uncertain.

31: the whole question is enclosed in square brackets in the edition, apparently marking it as doubtful or interpolated; the closing bracket is missing. 32: κυψέλαι taken as earwax. 33: ἀκμαί ('acmes') is a pun on ἀκμή, the prime of life. 34: the end of this passage is evidently corrupt (πυκνώδες, the broken clause ὅσῳ γὰρ συστρέφεται πρὸς ἑαυτὰ αἰτίων, ὑπομιμνῆσκον, ἐπακολουθεῖ τὴν αἰτίαν); the translation follows the words as closely as possible, and the sense is uncertain. 28: the opening of the answer (Διότι μὲν οὐ μερίζεσθαι...) is syntactically awkward and is rendered loosely. 29: 'the air on the other side' takes τοῦ εἰς τὸ ἐναντίον ἀέρος in its most likely sense.

35.1: The quotation is Homer, Iliad 1.317. 38.1: The text seems disturbed; 'aegilops' (αἰγίλωψ, a fistula at the inner corner of the eye, here evidently involving the nasal bone) is kept as a transliteration, and 'in the nature of the bones' renders an awkward phrase. 44.1 and 45.1: the bracketed sentences are bracketed in the edition, and 45.1 'ἀναπνοή' is taken as 'vent'. 51.1: the question is elliptical, literally 'Why the misshapen also senseless?'.

54.1: 'stomach' (στόμαχος) here means the gullet, βρόγχος the windpipe, ἀρτηρία the trachea. 57.1/58.1: πῶρος rendered 'callus' (bone callus). 61.1: stray 'b' in ἐπιτεb ταμένην is a footnote mark. 62.1: text corrupt in 'αἱ ποιότητος δίεφθειραν ... διέφθειραν' (dittography; read αἱ ποιότητες); 'tempered water' renders τὸ εὔκρατον. 63.1: the bracketed [μὴ] is needed for sense. 67.1: text garbled (ἀλλοιοῦνῷ ... φλυσιν ... ͅ11 μετρον); read ἀλλοιοῦνται; ὅτι τὸ ... κατὰ φύσιν ὂν καὶ σύμμετρον. 70.1: τεγνοπα2ο θοῦσι read as στεγνοπαθοῦσι ('constrictive affections', Methodist term). 69.1 θερητῶν and γίνεαι read as θεωρητῶν, γίνεσθαι.

73: στομάχου here likely means the stomach/gullet; at 80 rendered 'oesophagus' (στομάχου τὸ πέρας). The final sentences of 73 are obscure and the rendering is tentative; 'ὑδροφοβικοί' at the end of 80 seems odd in context (perhaps a corruption for another class of patients). 74: ἐκ read as ἐν. 81: μέρυς read as μέρος, συμπέῃ as συμπέσῃ. 79: ποροποιΐα 'pore-formation' is unusual; sense uncertain.

nodes.text: 1. Why are round ulcers harder to heal than the others? Now the Herophileans give the cause using a geometrical proof. They say that the circular shapes of ulcers look small in their perimeter, but are not so; rather they have in effect a larger area than they appear to. And what is larger needs more time to scar over, so that such ulcers naturally prove hard to heal even though they look small; in truth it is not so, but they are larger. Asclepiades, however, refuted this with circumspection: if, when a round ulcer is present, one cuts further into the adjacent tissues, so that from the further incision the shape of the ulcer becomes more elongated, the scarring over would happen faster. And this is contrary to Herophilus' doctrine. For if the size of the ulcer, as they themselves say, is the cause of the difficulty of treatment, then, with the same size remaining and another [size] being added from the further incision, these ulcers ought to become still harder to cure. Asclepiades himself gives the following cause. He says that in every thing to which motion is natural, the more vigorous motion arises from its own starting points; and by starting points he means the middles of the things in motion. For clarity he uses as examples the motion of rivers and that of fire. For as in these the middle parts move most and most vigorously, so it happens also with ulcers. What is meant is something like this: in rivers the motion becomes more vigorous at the part where there is most [water]; and clearly the middle is where there is most in them, for there the greater amount most converges. The same account holds for the flame of fire: for it moves most vigorously in the middle region, so much so that the flame often leaps up first at this part. Since, then, round ulcers too are, as it were, drawn together, and are, so to speak, towards the middle on every side, for this reason the motion in them comes to be more vigorous. And motion clearly occurs when certain corpuscles are naturally carried outwards through the pores, and by the vigorous passage of these the scarring over happens to be repelled. Against this it must be said that if the vigorous outward motion of the corpuscles is the cause of such ulcers being hard to heal, this ought to happen most in those in their prime, and in them such ulcers would result from these [causes]; for in them the corpuscles are especially quick-moving and great in number, whereas in the aged they are few and move sluggishly; yet generally in the latter such ulcers become harder to heal. It must be said, then, that in ulcers formed in a shape that is, as it were, angular, scarring over happens faster, because the healthy tissues are closer to one another, especially where the ulcer forms something like an angle. And healthy tissues contribute in no small way to scarring over. This is clear from the fact that ulcers are easier to cure when the tissues adjacent to them are healthy, rather than seeming healthy but in fact affected. In round ulcers, however, the healthy tissues stand equally distant from the ulcer on all sides, and farther than happens with an angular shape. Just as, if on a circle we took certain points a short distance apart and joined them with a straight line through the points, and likewise on another figure, say a triangle, joined [points] set a short distance from the angle, the straight line joined in the circle is found to be longer; so it is also with round ulcers and those that are not such, as we said. For this reason scarring over comes about easily in those formed in an angular shape, because the healthy tissues are closer to one another and contribute to the scarring over. Hence too scarring over generally begins from the extremities, since there it is most assisted by the adjacent healthy tissues. But in round ulcers, because the healthy [tissues] stand equally far from one another on all sides and cannot help in the scarring over, it does not come about easily.

Why are the extremities of the body, and likewise the hollow parts, susceptible to spreading ulceration? Is it because spreading ulceration is a kind of mortification and putrefaction, and the extremities are easily chilled through lack of matter, so that for this reason they undergo mortification; while the hollow parts, because moist matter abounds in them, for this reason undergo putrefaction?

Why, when ulcers are healing and inflammations are thinning, does itching occur? It must be said: because what is proper [to the body] then prevails. And in prevailing it drives out what is foreign from the depth; and nature takes pleasure when what is foreign is separated off.

Why does thirst occur in those with dropsy, although much fluid is present? It must be said that this craving arises from a seeking after the natural fluid, not the unnatural. And what is present in these [patients] is unnatural. The craving finds relief when natural fluid is supplied. Or [it is] because the natural fluid is not distributed into the pores that need it, but is pushed out. So they thirst as if they had not drunk.

Why, if we enter a bath when we are not thirsty, does thirst come on, and conversely, if we are thirsty, does the thirst stop? Because thirst arises from dryness. If, then, we enter the bath when thirsty, the body, because it partakes of vital power, as it were draws in the fluid through the pores of the surface, and so the depth, from which thirst chiefly arises, comes to be moistened. But in those who are not thirsty and enter the bath, fluid is present in the body, and this is given off through sweating, because [the body] does not lay claim to moisture.

Why, in those suffering in the liver, spleen or lung, is lying on the affected side easier? Yet one would expect the pains to grow more intense when the parts are pressed. But it must be said that if one lies on the opposite side, a kind of hanging down occurs; and when the affected parts hang down, the lying becomes greater.

Why, for the most part, do the extremities grow cold in paroxysms? Because the matters converge towards whatever place the starting point of the motion is in. And the starting point of the motion is in the depth of the middle parts. It is natural, then, that as matter converges on this part from every part of the body, the extremities too are stripped of the matter contained in them, and it is carried towards the middle. For once stripped and left in want of matter, they undergo chilling.

Pleasure is a kind of diffusion and relaxation of the body, and sensation itself in a way attests this. It is clear that pleasure also arises when sleep occurs. Experience bears witness to this, and so does the Poet, who in many places calls it 'sweet', as being productive of pleasure. If, then, pleasure is a diffusion of the body, and sleep produces this, why do we not rather call sleep relaxing than condensing, as the Methodists think? Moreover, rocking in a boat is relaxing, and when people take it they become somewhat sleepy, sinking off with a certain pleasure; so that from this too one may infer that sleep is relaxing rather than restraining. Or to this it must be said that pleasure is not strictly an attribute of sleep, but that when sleep occurs pleasure comes about because bodies are restored to their proper state, the fatigue from the activities of waking being, as it were, relieved. That pleasure does not always arise through the diffusion of bodies can be found from this: thirst arises from dryness, and dryness produces condensation. So when we are thirsty and sometimes take cold water, we feel great pleasure, even though the pre-existing density is intensified by the admixture of the cold. And just as we do not call cold relaxing because it produces pleasure in bodies, so neither would we call sleep relaxing because it is productive of pleasure. For pleasure arises, as we said, through the cause stated. Rocking in a boat can be dispersive of the coarse-particled bodies, but condensing of the sensory pneuma, clouding it and contracting it because of the stillness of the other matters. And when this is contracted, sleep comes on. Nor should one wonder if the same rocking disperses the body but condenses (as we said) the sensory pneuma. For just as hot water relaxes our bodies, yet if poured on fire puts it out, so rocking too produces opposite effects. And one could find many things able to bring about opposite effects.

Why is it that in wounds of the head, when the cut goes so deep that the meninx too is wounded, and the patients have survived and the wounds have by now come to scar over, convulsion sometimes occurs, so that those who suffer this even die? It must be said, then, that since the brain naturally pulsates, the meninx happens to rub against the surrounding bones, from which the removed pieces were taken away, and through rubbing it becomes ulcerated; and when ulceration has occurred, and it has become foul, and the matter collected from the ulceration cannot transpire (because the overlying tissues have already grown flesh, and also because the scar that has formed is denser), this matter (I mean the matter collected from the ulceration) moves to the principal parts of the brain and produces compression, so that convulsion also follows, since the matters cannot transpire, because the scar, being an unnatural growth of flesh, becomes hard.

It has been observed everywhere that, of wounds about the head deep enough that a division of the bones occurs, those about the crown and the bregma are more dangerous, but once they have come to scar over, they prove easier to heal than wounds that have arisen about the occiput. It must be said that the parts about the bregma, being more principal, have a thin meninx lying over them, and for this reason it is natural that the part is dangerous; but once they have come to scar over they are easier to heal, because the cooperation of the more principal parts becomes more vigorous. Those about the occiput are less dangerous, because the meninx lying over these places is fleshy, but harder to heal, because they neither receive any such cooperation, and moreover a coming-together [of the wound] dries out the parts.

This too has been observed, that in those who have such wounds about the head, if the bowel happens to be loosened spontaneously, death follows; but if it is by reason of the regimen, it gives promise of recovery. Because if the belly discharges spontaneously, having its origin in the head on account of the affection, it threatens danger, since the affection is overcoming nature; but if it has been moistened by reason of the regimen, as the matter is thinned and passed down to the lower parts, the parts about the head remain undisturbed, and so, with no heaviness accompanying, they become easy to heal.

Why does the heat from a charcoal fire for the most part cause headache, while that of wood does not? Because the excessive heat from charcoal condenses through a kind of dryness, while that from wood also has some moisture, which is shown by the smoke itself. For smoke is indicative of the moisture in the wood. One should quench the charcoal in a little wine, so that the harm that arises from it does not follow from it.

Why are pterygia especially prevalent among sea workers? For they occur in others too, but are prevalent among those who work at sea. It must be said, then, that there are two kinds of pterygia: for they arise sometimes when the flesh that naturally lies at the corner of the eye extends, or from joint growth, and sometimes when the thin membrane stretched around [the eye] becomes callous and swells. This [membrane] is hard to see in humans because of its extreme thinness, but in animals, and especially in lambs, it is very evident, being thicker; not so, however, in a human. This membrane, then, is eaten into by the sea vapours, which are rather sharp, and it undergoes callousing with inflammation, so that when it has thickened from this the affection of pterygium arises. We know that there are two kinds of pterygia: some are attached, others as it were grown together.

Why are affections of one eye more stubborn? Is it that when the other eye is in its natural state and moves with a natural motion, the affected one moves along with it, because their nature comes from a single base, and for this reason it irritates the affected one by the joint motion? For the ailing one needs rest. But when both are affected at the same time, the affection becomes milder. For each rests at the same time and is not irritated; and so from the rest a quick recovery of strength follows.

Why is it that in some who have ophthalmia, if fever comes on, it resolves it, while in others it not only does not resolve it but even produces complete blindness? What then is the cause of its healing some and destroying [the sight of] others? Because fever comes on by reason of a kind of *metasynkrisis* (re-arrangement of the body's compound), and if it is moderate, since the *metasynkrisis* produced by it is also moderate, benefit follows. But if it attacks violently, since the motion also becomes more violent, the utmost harm follows. One might also say that fever is drying; and that it is drying one can see from the thirst that accompanies those with fever; and that it also causes deposits is shown by the fact that, when it comes on, some of the parts suffer excessively. And the benefit arises when the fever happens to be drying, because the oncoming flux is dried up. But when it harms, it is one that causes deposits, both because the affected parts, being more susceptible, receive more, and because, being one that causes deposits, it fixes [the matter] there. And so the blindness arises from the abundant deposit.

Why does ophthalmia occur more in summer than in the other seasons, even though this season is dry and warm? For one would expect that, because dryness accompanies the season, no flux would arise, and that it should not occur through constriction either, because of the warmth present. It must be said that, although these things do accompany it, nevertheless the brightness, being great, harms the eyes more, because everything white beyond the mean is disturbing and confusing. Thus, when we prescribe rest, we order it to be taken in a dark part of a place, so as to avoid every condensing cause. In summer, then, the cause of ophthalmia, as has been shown, is the brightness of the sun.

Why, though there is a likeness between the eyes and the ears, does eye suffer along with eye, [but ear no longer with ear]? Because in the eyes there is not only likeness but also great nearness; while with the ears the distance between is great. And because the things that move the eyes together take their origin from within, while with the hearing [they] fall upon it from outside.

Why do some who have had ophthalmia see more sharply? Or is it clear that, for the reason that tear-producing eye-salves are called sharpeners of sight, because from the shedding of tears and, so to speak, purging, those who use them see more sharply, so too with those who have shed tears from ophthalmia, it happens that they see better, a purging having taken place of a thicker matter lying over [the eye]?

Why is it that in those about to develop cataract, gnat-like, fly-like and ant-like things, and whatever usually accompanies [this], are seen? Or is it clear that whatever sort of congealing the fluid takes, such things must also appear as soon as the fluid begins to congeal? And further, the visual faculty acts with the same application through the whole visual [organ]; but it is obstructed in those parts where the congealing chiefly occurs. So whatever shape the first-congealed part of the fluid happens to take, such too are the perceptions of the external objects.

Why do those who are yawning hear less? Because when the jaws are parted, the hearing is compressed, and at the same time pneuma is held in, whence noises also arise. So since the outside air has no entry, no perception occurs.

Why, when we probe our ears with ear-probes or some other things, does a cough happen to be stirred, as if the windpipe were irritated? Or is it because there is a great kinship, not only of the voice with the hearing, but also of the parts with the parts, so that the vocal organ too is affected in sympathy? And the coughing occurs in the vocal organ.

For what reason do some of those with headache perceive sounds keenly, while others do not perceive them at all? Or is it clear that, if the headaches become violent, so that a greater wedging occurs, with dizziness preceding, the mind happens not to be in its natural state; and "mind sees", as one of the ancients says; so that when this is impaired, and the sounds are present, they naturally do not perceive the sounds?

Why do those who are deaf speak through their nostrils? It is clear that from the very beginning of the affection perceptions arise in them as they widen the hearing passages, as it were, as far as they can; and as these widen, the passages of the nostrils, which were closed, are also widened by the distension. And so, as the pneuma is carried through by the distension, a kind of sound is easily produced.

Why do excessive sleep and sleeplessness, when they go on for long, produce heaviness in the head? And one cannot say that they harm the body as excesses do; for that is not what is being asked, namely why the head is harmed by opposites, but why exactly the same symptom follows from both sleeplessness and excessive sleep, though they are opposites. It must be said, then, that from excessive sleep this happens because the matter sent up into the head cannot be breathed out through [the skin], on account of the density that comes from sleep. In sleeplessness the same thing is brought about for the following reason: as the materials are thinned by the activities of waking, certain vapours are given off into the higher parts (and so also into the head); and as the matter is thinned more by intense sleeplessness, the giving-off also happens to be greater. And from sleeplessness it also happens that the food is not managed properly, but turns towards corruption; so that the very vapours given off into the head weigh it down not only by their quantity, but also because the food has turned for the worse.

Why are those who stay awake in the light of the moon not harmed by it at all, even if they happen to spend a long time in it, while those who sleep in it suffer wedging in their heads? Or is it clear that, since its light is at once warm and moist, those who sleep in it are weighed down in their heads? Or does this happen because the light falls upon sleepers in the manner of a blow, since it is bound up with a heaviness that comes from moisture, as with those who are douched with a forceful dashing? For in their case, because of the dashing, the inflows become like blows, so that wedging rather than loosening occurs. So in the same way, as the light of the moon also falls with heaviness for the reason stated, wedging or heaviness happens, the condensation from sleep also contributing.

Why do those who take gentle exercise, even if their heads are rather heavy before the exercise, have them relieved after the exercise, while those who move at a run, and did not previously feel any heaviness, have heavy heads after the exercise? It must be said that in those who take gentle exercise the materials happen to be drawn off gently to the lower parts; but in those who take strenuous exercise rebounds also occur, so that the materials carried to the lower parts are sent back up again when a rebound happens; just as it is with round things thrown on the ground. For here, if someone lets them go gently onto the ground, they stay and do not rebound; but if someone throws them with violence, they are carried upward again, as can be seen with balls. The same thing happens with runners, the matter being carried upward again in this way by the recoil. And also because in violent movement the pneuma happens to be held in and strained, so that for this reason too relief does not come about.

Why do movements in a straight line not cause dizziness, while circular ones do, and to such a degree that one thinks all external things are turning round along with one? Because, it must be said, movements made in a straight line do not prevent the breathing-out of matter, while circular ones do not allow the breathing-out to happen, since the air strikes more violently and prevents it. And the materials within us also happen to move in a circle like the movement that took place; for being carried along with the body and unable to be breathed out for the reason stated, the materials move in a circle even when the cause of the movement has ceased. And such movement in them is an unnatural perception: just as the jaundiced perceive the colours of external things according to the affection in their eyes, and likewise those with bloodshot eyes think everything reddish, so it is in circular motion, when people think everything is whirling round; for since the materials about the eyes are still whirling in a circle, the perception happens according to this affection. This is quite clear, because the eye contains fluids: the watery one, from which the tear comes, and the crystalline and the glassy; and all these are fluid, translucent and whitish. Besides these, clearly, the first coat is white; for this reason it is thinned in the middle of the eye, where it appears black; but it is not of that colour, as we say, but is wholly translucent at this part too. This too is known, that the second coat, being black by nature, is spread beneath the horny coat not over every part, but has a conspicuous opening, where the pupil appears. From all these things, then, the question is made clear.

Why, when people press up either the upper or the lower eyelid of the eye, do the objects before them happen to appear double? This happens especially also to those who have taken part in drinking. Because the visual pneuma is not divided — and this does not happen without the pressing — when in seeing the pneuma from both [eyes] falls jointly upon the external object; but when one eye is pressed, they no longer fall jointly upon the object, but each eye separately on its own. And this can be grasped, if one wishes, in this way: while the finger pressing the eye is still in place, if one closes the other of the two, that is, the one not being pressed, putting a hand in front of it, things no longer appear double, even though the pressing goes on. So the division of the pneuma is the cause in such cases, just as with drunken people the objects are seen multiplied.

Why, when we are in water, do we not perceive the voice, as we do through walls, although the things separating [us] are more solid? Because in water a kind of exact closing takes place, so that the air cannot slip in. But when we speak through walls, since the separating thing does not lie against the hearing, it is natural that, as the air on the other side is struck and the impulse is passed on through the air contained in the wall, the air happens to be struck, so that from this the perception of the word arises.

Why do swellings by the ears, which some also call Dioscuri, as arising for the resolution of ills, generally appear at the decline of severe diseases? We know that in severe diseases loss of appetite occurs; but once people have regained strength, they become more eager for food. And when more food is taken, there is movement of the jaws; and from the separation [of the parts] in chewing an inflammation arises; and when the inflammation settles as a deposit, swellings by the ears are produced.

[Why do turned-back ear lobes signify death in diseases? The cause is this: as the blood is extinguished, it is likely that greater dryness occurs about these, because these parts are by nature dry and poor in blood. This happens in a similar way to what happens with leather straps; for in the same way that with these the loss of moisture becomes the cause of a kind of curling, so it happens also with the lobes.

Why does earwax, which is naturally bitter, become sweet in those who are dying? Because it shows a great change from the natural state to its opposite, especially since [the earwax] is an exact test of sweet and bitter.

Why do pimples appear on the face at the time of the prime of life, so that some laymen even call them 'acmes'? These, as we said, appear over the whole face, but are most abundant about the nose. It is quite clear, then, that this happens from growth; for at this time attachment and accretion take place from the food. And while each of the parts changes the food that reaches it according to its own power, the parts about the face, and especially those about the nose, cannot change all that is supplied into flesh; and so the surplus of the food going to it happens to be changed into something foreign. That the cause of their formation is that the parts have little flesh is clear from the fact that pimples do not appear on the lips, because these parts are fleshy.

It must be asked for what reason, when cold water is applied to the nostril in a nosebleed, a greater flow of blood occurs, although cold is by nature more condensing. It must be said, then, that the bodies and vessels about the nose are easily broken. So when condensation occurs, some parts happen to be condensed and contracted, while others are stretched. For insofar as they contract upon themselves [...] causes; or else, when there is an underlying readiness for the flow, the water when applied affects the body along with it, recalling that it comes from this, and so the flow of blood follows the cause.

Why, with aromatics being burned as incense, do those far from the fire on which the aromatics have been thrown perceive [them] more than those nearby? It is quite clear that the fragrance becomes more potent when mixed with the surrounding air; for so the poet too said: 'And the savour reached heaven, whirling about in the smoke.' And it is reasonable that the fragrance becomes more perceptible to those at a distance; for being made finer it stirs sensation more.

Why, when we often have difficulty in sneezing, if we turn towards the light of the sun, does the sneeze come easily? What, then, is the cause? Because the sun's ray, falling on the inner parts of the nose, stirs up the sneeze like a little splinter, irritating the pores. Or is it that sneezes occur when pneuma runs beneath and irritates the parts? And the ray, warming what is in the nose, vaporises it more and assists the pneuma. If this becomes stronger, it brings about the sneeze more quickly, having irritated the bodies.

Why does a single sneeze rarely occur, and many rarely, but sneezes most often come in twos? The cause is obvious: for the pores of the nose are also two; and since a sneeze occurs by an expulsion of pneuma, when the one sneeze takes place through one pore, the other is affected along with it.

One might ask for what reason, when a fracture with bowing occurs in the limbs, flesh grows from within the sawn-off bone in such a way as to fill up the firmness between the bones and to match it; but in the case of aegilops, if a crushing of the bone occurs in the nature of the bones, the parts remain without growing flesh? Or is it that in the limbs the surrounding bodies are more numerous, and besides they have continuity with one another and are not separated from one another; but in the nose the parts have little flesh and lack continuity, and the space between is empty.

Why, when the air becomes frosty, does the fluid appear very thin and copious through the nostrils, although it ought to come out thicker because of the congealing from the cold? Because an excessive condensation occurs about the face, and the fluid is carried, as if by a kind of filtering, from the parts adjoining the nose, and so it happens to be thin.

Why, when an injury from striking occurs, do the parts close by not share the affection, while those far removed are affected along with it, as the groins with injuries to the feet? Asclepiades, then, in his work On Ulcers, says that at first matter is carried towards the parts struck, and as it is carried, as much as the affected parts can receive passes into them; but when these are filled and cannot take in a further quantity, the matter being carried overflows and, not received by the parts to which it was carried, is then carried on, and if it meets hollow places, stays in them, just as is the case with waters. For these, as long as they run on level ground, move evenly; but when they meet hollow places, they stay in them. The same thing, then, happens with the matter carried to the parts struck. For as much as [they] can receive passes into them; but the rest falls into hollows, and especially into the groins, which have open pores, and swells them. This explanation, then, is also plausible; but one might also blame the great susceptibility of the sinewy [tissue]; for this, through its excessive susceptibility, shares the affection of the affected parts sooner than the other parts of the body. It is for this reason, at any rate, that scrofulous swellings also form in the glands about the neck when there are ulcers about the head, and swellings in the armpit when there are ulcers about the hand.

Why, in the head, when the meninx is wounded on the right side, is the left side paralysed; and if this happens on the left, the right suffers the paralysis? It must be said that the cause is the position of the nerves. For these have their origin from the base of the brain. And they lie crosswise to one another: those arising from the right parts of the base run to the left parts of the head, and those arising from the left parts run to the right parts, so that their arrangement is crosswise. Reasonably, then, when someone is wounded on the right side of the meninx, the left side is paralysed; and in the other case the opposite.

Why in wars does the fall occur towards the wound? For it has been observed that the fall occurs towards the part that suffers the wound: for instance, if the wound happens to be in the front parts, the fall is not onto the back but onto the front. It must be said that the movement is towards whatever side nature limps: for instance, the nature of the body is in a kind of equilibrium and wishes to stand evenly. If, then, something happens to strike it and move it so that it limps, it is carried towards the side on which it limps; which happens also with leaning walls. For with these, even if someone wishes to set something against them from the opposite side so as to resist the lean, they nevertheless fall towards the side to which the lean has occurred; and especially if you use too forceful a blow in propping it.

Why do blisters rise on living people when burned, but not at all on the dead? It must be said that in living bodies pneumata are somehow dispersed throughout the whole body, but in the dead not at all; or that the bodies of the dead are inflexible, while those of the living are such as both to undergo stretching and to be able to be stretched. So when fire is applied, a drawing of matter to the surface occurs and produces the blisters. In dead bodies, then, these do not occur, because what gives substance to the blister is not present in them.

Why does sneezing alone not occur in us at night when we are in a natural state, or only rarely, while practically all other things [occur] both by day and by night? Or is it that sneezing is produced by some heat that has stirred the place from which it arises? That is why we also look up towards the sun when we want to sneeze; but when we sleep the heat is drawn away in the opposite direction. That is why the lower parts of sleepers become much warmer. Reasonably, then, we do not sneeze when the heat has departed from the head, which naturally stirs the fluid there, by whose expulsion the sneeze occurs. [And it is likely that the resulting affection does not occur.]

Why, when we rub the eye, do we stop sneezing? Or is it because this provides a vent for the fluid? For the eye waters after the rubbing. [And sneezing is due to an abundance of fluids. Or is it because a lesser heat is destroyed by a greater?] And the eye, when rubbed, gets more heat than that in the nose. For these reasons too, if one rubs the nose itself, the sneezing stops.

Why do the old, and not children, bear fasting? Because old age is sluggish, as being chilled; but infants are very hot and very active. And movement disperses; and those who are being dispersed need food.

Why after death, when all the limbs are relaxed, are the testicles alone drawn up? Because people emit semen in dying; and semen is usually discharged with the testicles drawing up, and so they remain held up.

Why do drunkards drink poor wine with pleasure? Because heavy drinkers have wide pores. So the thin, finest wine runs up through the large pores without being perceived; but the poor wine, being thick, stops and stays, and then seems to provide the pleasure that comes from it.

Why do angry people go red in the face, but frightened people turn pale? Anger is a sudden rushing out of the pneuma, fear a drawing back; hence where it is in excess it inflames, and where it is lacking it chills.
Why do some elderly people go bald, but others do not? Because some are hotter than others; for those who are chilled do not produce hair.
Why are the misshapen also senseless? Because the soul shares the affections of the body, just as the body those of the soul.
Why are large ulcers fatal when they are cleaned out during treatment? Because the psychic pneuma escapes unnoticed through many pores.

Why do those suffering from periodic illnesses shiver in hot weather? Because when the pores are opened, the heat escapes outwards; but when they are closed, it is shut in. So when the heat within us has gone out, chilling occurs; and shivering fits arise as the bodies contract through cold.

Why do we choke when we swallow solid food? Because the windpipe lies in front of the gullet, running alongside it lengthwise. So when this [the gullet] is filled, it presses on the trachea and stops the breath.

Why is white earth for the most part barren? Because it is very cold, while black [earth] is very hot; and the one generates reptiles (and these are cold), the other fruits (and these are hot). And indeed among women too, the dark ones are for the most part prolific, because of the greater heat in them.
Why do infants run more violent fevers? Because they are very hot; and fever is an intensification of the innate heat.

Why is it a sign that bones have formed callus that the bandages become stained with blood, even though the fracture occurred without a wound? Because when the callus flows together, it squeezes the drops of blood scattered in the porous spaces of the bones.

How does callus form? In this way: substance from the food, transformed and carried to those places, produces such [effects], and what is called callus comes into being. For just as in the nostrils this transformation, when it arrives, becomes mucus, and in the breasts milk, so also in bones [it becomes] callus, because of such a structure and nature of the part. For the parts assimilate the food to their own nature, according to what they are naturally suited for, as in a garden with many plants. For though the water irrigating the plants is one, each receives the water according to the nature it has: for example wormwood makes the water brought to it akin to its own nature, and basil likewise, and so on. But as Andreas of Carystus says, the marrow, pouring into the cavities of the bones and congealing around the lips of the break in the bone, and hardening, becomes callus.

Why do those seized by cholera, when the affection intensifies, suffer cramps in the calves? It must be said that cholera is an affection of the stomach. And this is sinewy; so when it is markedly intensified it affects the muscles in us along with it; for the muscles are sinewy.

Why, when anointed with an astringent eye-salve, do people perceive the astringency less with their eyes closed, but perceive the astringency more sharply when they open them? Because closed eyelids make the horny coat keep still; so while the eyeball is still, the ointment, blocking the pores, gives a lesser perception of its own astringency; but when we open the eyelids, we naturally have a greater perception of the astringency. For by the continual movement of the eye the eyeball, rubbing against the eyelids, becomes a cause of heat, and when this is produced, the pores perceptible only by reason are loosened and widened; and when these are widened, they must receive, so to speak, the corpuscles of the eye-salve perceptible only by reason; whence it produces a more astringent effect. Or [is it] because, in moving the eyes about after the anointing, the eye-salve, whirled round together with the eyeball, is made fine? For things in motion are always apt to be made fine; so the finer it is made, the more perception of astringency it gives.

Why are the phrenitic and the mad stronger during their paroxysms and have their strength intensified? It must be said that they are emboldened by their derangement; and their body is hard to bend because of excessive constriction. For this reason, when they come to remission, they lose strength, not becoming worse from better, but because the constriction has relaxed.

Why, when mustard plasters are applied, do people redden more when the mustard has been ground with water and smeared on, but when it is ground with vinegar it no longer produces this in those affected? It must be said that those smeared with vinegar naturally undergo less scarification and reddening; for they are astringed on the surface, and [the vinegar], so to speak, glazes over the closing of the pores that it produces; hence it does not allow the mustard room to penetrate so as to reach the pores. Or [is it] because the pungency of the mustard is blunted by the admixture of the vinegar? For these qualities, when combined, destroyed each other's own extreme of quality, through each having lost its own strength. As can also be seen in the case of what is called tempered water; for this too, made of very hot water and cold, has by a certain blending lost the extreme qualities, and besides them some other quality has been produced. But those given mustard plasters with the mustard ground in water redden more [in the places] for the following reason: water, by being smooth and by moistening, widens the pores perceptible only by reason and lets the mustard penetrate. And it is, as was said before, hot, and helps the more in the opening of the pores. So naturally those given mustard plasters with vinegar redden less, those with water more.

Why is rainwater sweet, although drawn up from the sea? It must be said that sea water is in itself salty; and this is heavy. But it has rivers flowing into it. So the wind, drawing up water from the sea, does not draw off the thick [part], but the fine part in it, which is the sweet. Naturally then rainwater is sweet, even if it is drawn up from the sea. Or [is it] because the wind with its violent force, even if it draws up [the] sea water [itself], moves it, and when moved it becomes finer? For things in motion are always apt to be made fine. And what is fine is also sweet, as [not] composed of large corpuscles. Therefore rainwater is sweet.

Why does sea water, though salty, become sweeter when boiled a long time? It is boiled until reduced to a third. It must be said that sea water, composed of large corpuscles, is made fine when broken up by the fire. Having therefore undergone a change, through passing from thick to fine, by losing its former quality it has become sweet instead of salty.

Why do severely inflamed eyes give the sufferers a sensation of some roughness? Is the roughness produced by rheum forming and getting in under the upper eyelid? Or is it because the vessels that interweave the eyelid unevenly on the inside become swollen, and so bring on the roughness?

Why does rheum form in the eye? Is it produced because the membranes of the eye become excessively heated, as if from burning, and the heat that ought to be dispersed from the depth is held back through excess and the difficulty of dispersal through the pores? Or because the natural fluids in the eye, dried up and as it were parched by the local heating, produce the formation of rheum?

Why are the pulses altered in those with fever? [Because] what is in us by nature and in due measure, becoming excessive, made fine by division through the [greater] heat arising in the depth, and becoming quick-moving through its lightness, alters not only the pulses but also the breathing itself.

Why do those with fever have a surface that feels ulcerated? Because the flesh, rubbing against the retained corpuscles, being easily chafed, becomes irritated; as also tends to happen with those who have some part of the body inflamed.

Why do those with fever turn pale? This happens either through the alteration of the fluids in us, or through the change in the structure of the pores perceptible only by reason; and one must consider that the same holds analogously for the excretions of the bowels and the urine.

Why, in those with fluxional fevers, though there is dispersal and evacuation of what is in us, does a certain heat appear in them, and the pulse is large? Because the dispersal happens as the underlying matter is made very fine; and by the particular passage of the corpuscles and their friction, the particular heat is produced. And we do not say that those with fluxional fevers have heat like those with constrictive affections, nor indeed the pulse; but [only] by comparison with the healthy. This will be clear to you also from those who have bathed or exercised, in whom the pores are relaxed, and what underlies them happens to be made fine and the heat evidently to be breathed out; and [the heat] comes to be and is greater than is natural, and the pulse more forceful, and has size; for sluggishness and heaviness are produced by diminished strength.

Why do those who have had fever have no appetite for food? Is it because appetite consists in a certain proportion of the pores in the stomach and belly? And it is reasonable that this proportion does not remain sound, the pores either being dilated too far, or closing.

Why in cholera are the extremities contracted, cramped and chilled, and the pulse faint? Because the pneuma from them is imperceptibly dispersed towards the fine-partedness in the belly; for in these people the belly is very hot; hence they also go numb. And parts deprived of the supply of pneuma go numb; and the extremities are chilled and contracted, because the heat in them too is carried to the belly on account of its fine-partedness.

Why do those with hydrophobia fear water, and become tense in the genitals together with the hypochondria, and tremble and are convulsed and become deranged to such a degree that they even bark like dogs? They are convulsed and tremble because the stomach is linked with the sinewy [parts]. For the same reason they also become tense in the genitals. For the constitution and affection of one with hydrophobia is an obstruction about the stomach and the belly. They become deranged because corrupted matter is distributed to the belly and stomach, and some part of it is exhaled upward to the meninges. And lodging as an obstruction about these, it produces the fits of madness. They are troubled when they drink, because the build-up was formed about small pores. So when they drink, the water, being fine-parted, slips into the small pores and increases the obstructions. But they are not troubled by solid food. For its corpuscles, being large, the affected [pores] never admit. And even when not drinking water, they fear it because of the impression on the sense-organs. For one who drinks both sees and drinks at once; and the sight, moved by the water, moves along with it the pneuma in the mouth. And this, moved by what is drunk, moves the sight along with it in the same way as it was formerly moved by the water; and from this joint movement such a joint training arises that, even if the water is not drunk, pneuma is lodged in the stomach moving along [with the sight], as it was earlier troublesomely moved by what was drunk. So they drink with their heads covered, because one of the two movements is removed. And beyond this, [the water] passing on is better able to lodge in the pores of the stomach.

Why do those who have suffered indigestion belch up corrupted food? Because, owing to the quantity taken in, greater heat arises in the cavity of the belly; and this, being filled up, corrupts the food and makes it smell of burnt fat, not in the interstices but in the cavity.

Why do those who have headache have dim sight and weep continually? Because, as matter is carried up to the head (for matters are always carried to the affected parts), a large part is carried to the eyes, and this reasonably, because they are opened through the abundance of fine-partedness, which arises from their continual movement. And on the one hand they weep because of the quantity of matter loading the parts; on the other they have dim sight because the natural pneuma, which passes through the visual pores, is made turbid by admixture of the matter supplied.

Why do noises occur when there is headache? Because the auditory pneuma is shaken by the obstruction that has formed about the parts; and an obstruction is a corpuscle [lodged] in interstices perceptible only by reason, through wedging.
Why do those who have headache suffer more pain when they get up? Because when the head is moved, a greater flow of matter goes to it and increases the obstructions.
Why does pulselessness occur? Because, when the affection is malignant, pneuma is drawn from the arteries towards the fine-partedness in the affected parts.

Why do the mad become deranged? Because difficulty of passage of the psychic pneuma is produced, through obstruction and closing of the pores in the bodies that transform it; for the affection forms about the brain and the meninges there, and the offshoots from there, because they are in an unnatural state. And they are seen to have certain imaginings, and to see things not standing as standing, and things not existing as existing, suffering something similar to those with jaundice. For they too, because of the pore-formation of the pores produced in the eyes, have such an impression of visible things; for everything appears to them to be yellow-green.

Why are melancholics irascible and despondent? Because the affection settles about the belly and the end of the oesophagus, which joins the mouth of the belly. So when fluids are corrupted there, an accumulation is produced, and becomes the cause of what has been mentioned; this is clear also from those who are healthy but have just begun taking food. For they become hard to deal with. And those with hydrophobia, believing they are plotted against, almost stop eating.

Why, among paralysed parts, are some stretched out while others are drawn in and contracted? Because the affection is produced in the interstices perceptible only by reason. So when the closing occurs lengthwise, the paralysed part is stretched out; and it contracts when the pores close crosswise.

Why do those with difficult breathing make a whistling noise? Because the affection is a closing and collapse of the pores in the lung. So as the pneuma passes through a narrow place, such a noise is produced. Coughs also befall them, because of the heat from friction, as more corpuscles are passed into the hollows of the bronchi, and these are at the same time struck by the pneuma.

Why do those with difficult breathing have less difficulty breathing when upright than when lying down? Because, the windpipe being affected in respect of the breath, it helps that the chest also is raised up along with it.

Why, in ruptures of those ruptured by a blow, is the lower abdomen, which is outside, not ruptured, while the peritoneum, which is inside, is ruptured? The cause of this is the very nature of the bodies: the lower abdomen is fleshy, while the peritoneum is stretched taut; so, resisting what strikes it, it is ruptured. The same thing happens also with fractures without wounds.
